newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin away, Russian government faces tough fight.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin away, Russian government faces tough fight.

text.p: With President Boris Yeltsin away from the Kremlin, his government faced bitter battles on several fronts on Thursday and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin ordered his ministers to brace for surprises.
Russian news agencies said Chernomyrdin told a cabinet meeting all ministers had to attend a session of the State Duma lower house of parliament on Friday to defend the 1997 budget.
"You must be ready for every possibility. Anything could happen," Itar-Tass quoted him as telling ministers.
The opposition-dominated Duma, which rejected the cabinet's original draft budget, will discuss a compromise spending plan prepared by a government-parliamentary arbitration commission.
Chernomyrdin told ministers to defend the plan at the session, admitting that "the situation in the economy is very complicated, especially over payment of wages and pensions".
Experts predict the Duma is likely to reject the new draft.
The position of the communists, the largest single group in the Duma, is seen as decisive. Chernomyrdin met their leader, Gennady Zyuganov, on Thursday.
An unresolved conflict between the government and the Duma might lead to Yeltsin having to make a choice between dismissing one or other of the bodies.
Yeltsin, 65, who had a multiple heart bypass operation on November 5, was spending his first day at a country residence where he moved on Wednesday from the nearby Barvikha sanatorium.
The government also faces angry miners, hundreds of thousands of whom began a national strike on Tuesday demanding the government be replaced and that Moscow pay overdue wages.

In the biggest coalmining region, the Kuzbass in southern Siberia, the strike appeared to be losing momentum. But across Russia, Interfax news agency said, the number of mines on strike grew to 132 on Thursday from 124 on Wednesday.
Many of the miners have not been paid since April.

The Duma passed a resolution on Thursday, urging Yeltsin to sort out the situation in the mining industry and warning it would stage a no-confidence vote in the government if it did not move to resolve the conflict.
On a brighter note for Chernomyrdin, the Federation Council upper chamber of parliament failed to approve a recommendation to the Duma to stage a no-confidence vote.
Instead, the Council decided to meet in an unscheduled session on December 10 to consider Chernomyrdin's record.

On Wednesday, the normally compliant upper house was in uncharacteristic uproar against the prime minister after Chernomyrdin, pleading illness, refused to appear to explain how he planned to solve the economic crisis.
Some Council members, who are drawn from Russia's regional leaders, called for a motion of no confidence in Chernomyrdin's government and questioned its ability to handle the situation.
Several deputies demanded the government reverse its tight monetary policy and simply print cash to pay wages and pensions.

The liberal governor of Nizhny Novgorod region, Boris Nemtsov, told Council speaker Yegor Stroyev during the debate: "You've got to go to Chernomyrdin and ask him if he has the will and the courage to work on in this post or not."
The Council created another headache for Yeltsin on Thursday when it demanded Ukraine hand over the Black Sea naval port of Sevastopol, saying it was Russia's and Kiev had no right to it.
The move is likely to cause a storm of protest in Ukraine and disrupt delicate negotiations between the two governments.
The Kremlin said Yeltsin would meet Stroyev on Friday, though the speaker had said the encounter would be on Thursday.
